Poor walk test performance reflects frailty and limited physiologic reserve, which may correlate with complications including AKI but is not a direct renal mechanism.

Prior interventions suggest advanced CAD/valvular disease and potentially more complex redo surgery, indirectly increasing AKI risk. Still nonspecific relative to immediate postoperative perfusion and renal biomarkers.

ACE inhibitors can blunt efferent arteriolar tone and predispose to perioperative hypotension/renal hypoperfusion, especially in elderly patients. This is a recognized perioperative AKI risk modifier but not definitive alone.

Amiodarone is not a typical direct nephrotoxin and has weak direct linkage to postoperative AKI. It mainly reflects arrhythmia history rather than renal perfusion status.
Anticoagulants mainly influence bleeding risk and perioperative management; AKI linkage is indirect through hypotension/transfusion. Not a primary mechanistic predictor of creatinine rise.
Low-dose aspirin has minimal direct nephrotoxicity and is common standard-of-care in cardiac patients. Any AKI signal is weak and confounded by indication.
Beta-blockers can contribute to bradycardia/low cardiac output in some contexts, but overall are routine therapy and not a strong AKI predictor. Association is indirect via hemodynamics.
Chronic beta-blocker use is common and mainly reflects baseline cardiac disease management. It has no strong direct mechanistic link to postoperative creatinine ratio.
Chronic CCB therapy is not a recognized direct AKI driver in cardiac surgery. Any relationship is indirect and likely confounded by comorbidity patterns.
Often indicates recent ACS/high-risk PCI and increases bleeding/transfusion risk, which can secondarily affect renal perfusion. Not a direct renal injury marker.

Pre-op inotrope requirement signals low cardiac output/cardiogenic shock physiology, a well-established risk factor for renal hypoperfusion and postoperative AKI. Stronger prognostic value than most medication-history variables.
Statins/lipid-lowering therapy are not direct AKI triggers and are ubiquitous in this population. Any protective/harmful effect is small relative to perioperative hemodynamics.
Reflects angina management and CAD severity but does not directly predict renal injury. Indirect association is weak compared with perfusion and nephrotoxin exposures.
IV nitrates suggest active ischemia/heart failure and can contribute to hypotension, indirectly increasing AKI risk. Still nonspecific and less predictive than direct low-output markers.
Broad antianginal therapy history is a nonspecific proxy for CAD burden. It has weak direct mechanistic linkage to postoperative creatinine rise.

Chronic steroids can reflect frailty/immunosuppression and may worsen infection risk and glycemic control, indirectly increasing AKI risk. Not a direct renal perfusion marker, so kept low for sparsity.
Primarily affects bleeding/transfusion needs rather than renal perfusion directly. Any AKI association is indirect and inconsistent.
Warfarin exposure mainly influences perioperative bleeding and transfusion; renal effects are indirect. Warfarin-related nephropathy is uncommon and not a typical driver in this setting.
DOAC exposure is chiefly relevant to bleeding management; links to postoperative AKI are indirect. Not a strong physiologic predictor of creatinine rise.
Similar to other anticoagulants, this is more about bleeding/transfusion than kidney injury mechanisms. Weak and indirect relationship to postoperative creatinine ratio.
Statins may be modestly protective via anti-inflammatory effects, but evidence for predicting AKI after cardiac surgery is mixed. More a comorbidity/health-status marker than a direct predictor.
Recent catheterization can imply contrast exposure and higher baseline cardiovascular complexity, both associated with AKI risk. Still indirect without timing/contrast dose, so capped low.
Known coronary disease reflects vascular burden and potential low cardiac output risk, indirectly related to renal hypoperfusion. Not specific enough to strongly predict creatinine ratio.
Greater coronary disease burden correlates with operative complexity and risk of postoperative low-output states that can precipitate AKI. Association is indirect and confounded, so kept below 0.05.
Severe aortic valve disease can predispose to perioperative hemodynamic instability and low renal perfusion. However, it is not a direct biomarker and overlaps with other cardiac severity measures.
Mitral disease can be associated with pulmonary hypertension/low forward flow and higher surgical complexity, indirectly increasing AKI risk. Not a direct renal injury indicator.

Tricuspid disease/right-sided failure can cause venous congestion and elevated renal venous pressure, a recognized contributor to AKI. This is a more kidney-relevant hemodynamic phenotype than other valve lesions.
Pulmonic valve disease is uncommon and usually not a primary determinant of postoperative renal perfusion in adult cardiac surgery. Weak, nonspecific link to AKI.

Redo sternotomy often increases operative time/complexity and risk of bleeding/transfusion and low-output states, which can contribute to AKI. Still an indirect proxy rather than a physiologic renal marker.
Without clear clinical definition (e.g., elective vs emergent), this variable is hard to interpret mechanistically for AKI prediction. Treated as weak evidence to avoid spurious inclusion.
Case cancellation is an administrative/operational outcome and does not reflect postoperative renal physiology. No meaningful link to creatinine ratio at 60 hours.

Conversion (e.g., minimally invasive to open) is a marker of intraoperative complexity/complications, often associated with longer ischemic time, bleeding, and hemodynamic instability that increase AKI risk.
Robotic approach mainly reflects surgical technique and case selection; it has no direct physiologic linkage to postoperative renal injury beyond correlated factors.
CABG is associated with AKI risk via CPB exposure and perioperative hemodynamic shifts, but this binary label is a coarse proxy and overlaps with other operative severity markers.
Valve surgery can carry higher AKI risk due to longer bypass/cross-clamp times and postoperative low cardiac output, but procedure type alone is indirect and collinear with other severity indicators.
Additional cardiac procedures suggest greater operative complexity and inflammatory/ischemic burden, indirectly increasing AKI risk.
AF ablation/maze procedures add operative time but are not a primary driver of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity; effect is mostly indirect.
Aortic procedures are strongly associated with AKI due to prolonged CPB, hypothermia/circulatory arrest, embolic risk, and higher rates of postoperative shock.
Concurrent non-cardiac procedures may reflect complexity and longer anesthesia time, but the relationship to AKI is nonspecific and heterogeneous.
Appropriate prophylactic antibiotic choice is standard-of-care and not a direct determinant of early postoperative creatinine rise; nephrotoxicity is not captured by this appropriateness flag.
Timing of prophylactic antibiotics primarily affects surgical site infection risk rather than early AKI physiology; limited direct relevance to creatinine ratio at 60h.
Discontinuation orders reflect protocol adherence and clinician behavior more than renal perfusion or nephrotoxic exposure intensity.
Redosing is a proxy for longer operations or blood loss, which can correlate with AKI risk, but it is indirect and not a renal biomarker.
Lower nadir temperature can indicate deeper hypothermia/complex CPB strategies (e.g., circulatory arrest) associated with systemic hypoperfusion and higher AKI risk.
Intraoperative anemia reduces renal oxygen delivery and is linked to postoperative AKI, especially in elderly patients with limited renal reserve.
Perioperative hyperglycemia is associated with stress response and worse outcomes, but its link to AKI is indirect compared with hemodynamics and oxygen delivery.
Use of specialized perfusion strategies may correlate with operative complexity, but the directionality and renal impact are heterogeneous and largely indirect.

Aortic cannulation is common in routine CPB and is not independently predictive of renal injury beyond overall surgical complexity. Any AKI signal is better captured by CPB duration and circulatory arrest variables.

Femoral arterial cannulation can reflect higher-risk or redo/emergent cases and may be associated with more atheroembolism or malperfusion risk. Still an indirect proxy and largely collinear with operative complexity.

Axillary cannulation often indicates complex aortic surgery and altered perfusion strategies, indirectly increasing AKI risk. The primary mechanistic drivers are better represented by CPB and arrest times.
Innominate cannulation is typically used in complex arch/aortic procedures and may proxy for higher operative risk. It is not a direct renal perfusion biomarker.
Other cannulation sites are heterogeneous and mainly reflect procedural variation rather than a consistent renal risk mechanism. Limited interpretability reduces predictive value.
Femoral venous cannulation can indicate minimally invasive or complex access scenarios and may correlate with case complexity. It has no direct physiologic linkage to renal tubular injury.
Jugular venous cannulation site choice is usually technical and not a known driver of postoperative AKI. Any association is likely confounded by procedure type.
Right atrial venous cannulation is standard for many CPB cases and does not independently predict AKI. Renal risk is better captured by perfusion time and hemodynamic instability.
Left atrial venous cannulation is uncommon and procedure-specific, without a consistent mechanistic link to AKI. Likely reflects surgical approach rather than renal insult.
Pulmonary venous cannulation is rare and primarily technical/procedural. It is not an established predictor of postoperative renal dysfunction.
Bicaval cannulation may be used in more complex intracardiac procedures and can proxy for longer CPB or more inflammation. Still indirect and typically dominated by CPB duration effects.
This category is heterogeneous and unlikely to encode a consistent renal risk pathway. Any signal is likely noise or confounding by procedure type.

Longer CPB time is a strong, well-established risk factor for AKI via inflammation, hemolysis, nonpulsatile flow, and renal hypoperfusion. It also correlates with operative complexity and transfusion/vasopressor needs.

Use of circulatory arrest indicates major aortic/arch surgery with higher risk of global hypoperfusion and ischemia-reperfusion injury, increasing AKI risk. It is a strong marker of severe physiologic stress even if duration is captured separately.

Longer DHCA time directly increases risk of systemic ischemia and subsequent renal ischemia-reperfusion injury, a potent mechanism for postoperative AKI. Duration provides more granular risk than the binary arrest indicator.

Cerebral perfusion strategies are primarily neuroprotective and reflect complex arch surgery; renal implications are indirect through overall perfusion management. Any association with AKI is likely mediated by arrest/CPB duration and case complexity.

Longer selective cerebral perfusion time is a proxy for complex/prolonged aortic surgery and cardiopulmonary bypass exposure, which increases systemic inflammation and renal hypoperfusion risk. It is indirect (brain-focused) and partly collinear with other duration metrics.

Circulatory arrest implies profound global hypoperfusion/ischemia and typically longer bypass/complexity, which are established drivers of postoperative AKI. Duration is clinically meaningful and less redundant than cerebral monitoring variables.

Aortic occlusion indicates major aortic manipulation and potential embolic/ischemic burden, but as a binary flag it is a coarse proxy for complexity. Much of its signal is captured better by clamp/arrest times and transfusion needs.

Cross-clamp time is a well-established marker of operative complexity and ischemic/inflammatory burden during cardiac surgery, correlating with AKI risk. It is a stronger, more direct duration metric than cerebral oximetry use.

Use of cerebral oximetry reflects monitoring preference and case type rather than a physiologic insult causing AKI. It is not a direct renal perfusion marker and is likely confounded by institutional practice.

Diffuse aortic calcification reflects advanced atherosclerosis and higher risk of embolization and perioperative hemodynamic instability, which can contribute to AKI. The link is plausible but indirect and confounded by overall comorbidity burden.
Documentation of aortic assessment is largely procedural/behavioral and does not itself represent a renal insult. It mainly reflects standard operative evaluation and is weakly informative for AKI.

Plaque assessment is a documentation/assessment variable and not a physiologic driver of renal injury. Any association would be indirect via case complexity and is better captured by operative times and transfusions.

An altered surgical plan due to aortic condition suggests unexpected complexity and potentially longer bypass, more hemodynamic perturbations, and embolic risk, all associated with AKI. Still indirect and heterogeneous, so capped to avoid over-weighting.
Refusal of blood products is not a physiologic mechanism for AKI and is rare; any effect would be mediated through anemia/hypoperfusion but is highly confounded. Treat as weak evidence.

Receiving blood products is a marker of bleeding, hemodilution, and operative complexity, and transfusion is associated with postoperative AKI via inflammation and microcirculatory effects. This is an established but nonspecific risk factor.

RBC transfusion volume correlates with bleeding/anemia and is consistently associated with AKI after cardiac surgery, likely via inflammatory and storage-lesion effects plus severity confounding. More specific than the aggregate blood-products variable.

FFP transfusion indicates coagulopathy/bleeding and higher surgical complexity, which can accompany hypotension and renal hypoperfusion. Association with AKI is plausible but less consistent and more confounded than RBCs.

Platelet transfusion suggests significant bleeding or platelet dysfunction (often with prolonged bypass), both linked to higher AKI risk. It is an indirect severity marker and typically collinear with other transfusion measures.

Cryoprecipitate use reflects severe bleeding/hypofibrinogenemia and complex surgery, which can be associated with renal hypoperfusion and inflammation. It is relatively infrequent and largely a severity proxy.

Intraoperative clotting factor administration indicates coagulopathy/bleeding severity and complex operative course, indirectly increasing AKI risk through shock/transfusion burden. It is heterogeneous and overlaps with other transfusion indicators.

Antifibrinolytic use is not a direct renal insult and is usually driven by bleeding risk rather than kidney perfusion. Any AKI association is indirect via transfusion/bleeding severity and should be kept low for sparsity.
Tranexamic acid is not typically nephrotoxic; its use mainly reflects bleeding prophylaxis. Any relationship to AKI is indirect and confounded by surgical complexity.
TEE performance is standard in many cardiac surgeries and reflects monitoring practice rather than renal physiology. It has no direct mechanistic link to postoperative creatinine rise.

Residual aortic regurgitation can reduce effective forward flow and contribute to low cardiac output, indirectly worsening renal perfusion. However, it is an indirect marker and often mild/managed, so keep modest.
Residual MR can drive pulmonary congestion and low effective cardiac output, which can impair renal perfusion. It is a plausible but indirect AKI risk marker.

TR is closely tied to elevated right-sided pressures and venous congestion, which is a recognized contributor to cardiorenal syndrome and postoperative AKI. Residual TR can therefore be an established hemodynamic risk factor.

Valve surgery generally implies longer bypass/cross-clamp and higher hemodynamic complexity, which can increase AKI risk. Still, this is a coarse proxy and likely collinear with other severity markers.
Concomitant AF procedures may increase operative time and complexity, indirectly increasing AKI risk. The link is weak and largely confounded by overall surgical burden.
General anesthesia is nearly universal in cardiac surgery and provides little discrimination for AKI risk. It is not a specific renal risk factor in this context.
PCC use signals major bleeding/coagulopathy and high-acuity surgery, which can be associated with hypotension/transfusion and AKI. The relationship is indirect and confounded, so keep below 0.05.

Higher residual aortic gradients can reflect suboptimal valve hemodynamics and potential afterload/low output states, indirectly affecting renal perfusion. Typically a weaker predictor than direct perfusion/pressure measures.
Paravalvular leak can cause hemolysis and/or reduced effective forward flow, potentially contributing to renal injury. Usually an indirect and variable contributor, so modest importance.

Residual mitral stenosis/gradient may limit forward flow and contribute to congestion, indirectly affecting renal perfusion. Generally a weaker, indirect predictor compared with direct hemodynamic/lab markers.
Mitral PVL can lead to hemolysis and heart failure physiology, both of which can worsen renal function. Still typically an indirect marker and not a definitive AKI driver.

Combined residual AV valve regurgitation suggests persistent volume overload/low effective output and venous congestion, which can predispose to AKI. This is an indirect but clinically plausible risk indicator.

Lower post-procedure EF is a strong indicator of low cardiac output risk, a key mechanism for postoperative renal hypoperfusion and AKI. It is an established hemodynamic predictor, though not kidney-specific.

Planned PCI mainly reflects coronary disease complexity and potential contrast exposure, but it is an indirect and inconsistent driver of postoperative AKI compared with direct hemodynamic/renal markers.
Need for IABP indicates perioperative low cardiac output/cardiogenic shock physiology, which is an established risk factor for renal hypoperfusion and subsequent AKI.
Catheter-based assist suggests higher acuity and possible hemodynamic instability, but the relationship to creatinine rise is indirect and heterogeneous across devices/indications.
ECMO use is a strong marker of severe cardiopulmonary failure with high rates of renal hypoperfusion, inflammation/hemolysis, and fluid overload, all strongly linked to AKI.
Blood product transfusion burden correlates with bleeding, inflammation, hemolysis, and hemodynamic instability; transfusions are an established postoperative AKI risk factor in cardiac surgery.
Extubation in the OR is a proxy for physiologic stability and lower illness severity; it is indirectly associated with lower AKI risk but not a direct renal mechanism.
Re-intubation reflects respiratory failure and clinical deterioration often accompanied by hypotension, higher vasopressor needs, and fluid shifts, which increase AKI risk.
ICU visit/transfer is largely standard postoperative workflow after cardiac surgery and provides little specific mechanistic information about renal injury risk.
Lower postoperative hemoglobin can reduce oxygen delivery and may reflect bleeding/transfusion needs; it has a plausible link to renal ischemia but is not a specific AKI biomarker.
Postoperative hematocrit overlaps strongly with hemoglobin and mainly reflects anemia/hemodilution; it is an indirect marker and adds limited independent AKI signal.
Remaining intubated postoperatively is a proxy for higher acuity and potential hemodynamic/respiratory instability, indirectly increasing AKI risk.
Prior MI indicates underlying ischemic cardiomyopathy risk and reduced cardiac reserve, which can predispose to low-output states and renal hypoperfusion postoperatively.
Timing of prior MI may correlate with cardiac reserve, but its incremental value beyond the presence of MI and perioperative hemodynamics is typically small for predicting AKI.
Symptom timing at admission is not directly linked to renal perfusion or nephrotoxic exposure and is unlikely to add meaningful AKI prediction beyond acuity/hemodynamics.
Symptom timing at surgery is a weak proxy for urgency and does not directly capture renal insult mechanisms; expected predictive value for creatinine rise is minimal.
Angina class reflects coronary disease severity and functional limitation, which may relate indirectly to perioperative cardiac reserve, but it is not a direct predictor of postoperative AKI.
Higher NYHA class reflects worse baseline cardiac reserve and propensity to low-output states post-op, indirectly increasing AKI risk. It is a coarse pre-op severity marker and not kidney-specific.

Cardiogenic shock implies profound renal hypoperfusion and venous congestion, both strong drivers of postoperative AKI. It is a direct hemodynamic collapse state closely linked to subsequent creatinine rise.
Need for resuscitation suggests perioperative instability (hypotension/bleeding/low flow) that can precipitate ischemic tubular injury. It is an established but nonspecific marker of severity.

Arrhythmias can reduce cardiac output and renal perfusion, but the umbrella term is heterogeneous and often transient/treated. Predictive value is indirect compared with shock or sustained hypotension.
VT/VF episodes indicate severe instability and potential low-flow periods that can cause renal ischemia. Still, effect depends on duration and hemodynamic impact, so it is not definitive alone.
Sick sinus syndrome mainly reflects conduction disease and pacing needs rather than renal perfusion injury. Any AKI association is weak and largely mediated by overall cardiac comorbidity.
Atrial flutter can impair cardiac output and contribute to congestion, but is often rate-controlled and less strongly linked to AKI than shock states. Thus it is an indirect predictor.
Second-degree AV block may cause bradycardia and reduced perfusion, but is frequently managed with pacing and may be transient. Association with AKI is plausible but weak.
Complete heart block can cause significant bradycardia/low output until paced, which can threaten renal perfusion. Predictive value is moderate but typically mitigated quickly with pacing.
Being paced is more a marker of conduction disease and postoperative management than a direct renal insult. Any AKI link is indirect via underlying cardiac dysfunction.

Heart failure is an established AKI risk factor via low forward flow and elevated venous pressures (cardiorenal physiology), especially after cardiac surgery. It meaningfully increases susceptibility to postoperative creatinine rise.

Atrial fibrillation can reduce effective cardiac output and is associated with postoperative complications and congestion, modestly increasing AKI risk. It is common and often controlled, so not highly specific.
Preoperative pain score has no direct physiologic linkage to renal perfusion or tubular injury. Any association would be confounded by overall illness or analgesic use and is weak.

Cell saver volume is a proxy for surgical blood loss/complexity and transfusion needs, which can correlate with inflammation and hypotension. However it is indirect and not a kidney-specific exposure.
Heparin dosing before bypass is largely protocol-driven and not a direct nephrotoxin. It has minimal mechanistic connection to postoperative creatinine rise.

Protamine can cause hypotension, pulmonary vasoconstriction, and hemodynamic instability in susceptible patients, which could secondarily impair renal perfusion. Dose is still an indirect and context-dependent predictor.
Viscoelastic testing (e.g., TEG/ROTEM) reflects coagulation management rather than renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity. Any association with AKI would be indirect via bleeding/transfusion complexity.
Use of a volatile anesthetic is common and not a specific driver of postoperative AKI. It may weakly proxy case/anesthesia complexity but has no direct renal biomarker role.
Isoflurane choice is unlikely to directly affect creatinine rise compared with hemodynamics, bypass time, and nephrotoxins. Any effect would be indirect through blood pressure management.

Sevoflurane has theoretical renal concerns (compound A) but clinically significant AKI signal in modern practice is weak, especially relative to perfusion/vasopressor exposure. Could modestly proxy anesthetic strategy.
Desflurane selection is not an established AKI predictor; renal outcomes are dominated by perfusion pressure, congestion, and inflammatory/bypass effects. Likely reflects provider preference.
Other volatile agents are heterogeneous and not mechanistically tied to AKI risk in a consistent way. This variable is more about documentation than renal physiology.
Pre-bypass volatile use is routine and not a direct determinant of postoperative creatinine trajectory. Any association would be confounded by overall anesthetic course and hemodynamics.
During-bypass anesthetic strategy may correlate with bypass management and inflammatory stress, but volatile use itself is not a strong AKI driver. At most a weak proxy for intraoperative course.
Post-bypass volatile use may correlate with hemodynamic instability and need for deeper anesthesia, indirectly relating to renal hypoperfusion risk. Still not a primary AKI predictor.
Maintenance volatile use is standard practice and not specifically linked to AKI compared with perfusion pressure, vasopressors, and fluid balance. Limited incremental prognostic value.
Dexmedetomidine can influence sympathetic tone and blood pressure, potentially affecting renal perfusion indirectly. Evidence for AKI prevention/causation is mixed, so relevance is low.
Propofol infusion mainly reflects anesthetic technique; renal impact is indirect via hypotension. Not an established independent predictor of postoperative creatinine rise.
Midazolam infusion is not mechanistically linked to AKI and largely reflects sedation practice. Any association would be confounded by case complexity.
Higher insulin requirement can proxy perioperative hyperglycemia/stress response, which is associated with worse postoperative outcomes including AKI. It is indirect and confounded, so kept low.

Preoperative systolic BP reflects baseline hemodynamic reserve and chronic hypertension, which increases susceptibility to renal hypoperfusion during surgery. It is an established but nonspecific AKI risk factor.
Diastolic BP relates to vascular tone and coronary/renal perfusion pressure and may reflect chronic hypertension/arterial stiffness in the elderly. Predictive value is plausible but indirect.
Pre-induction heart rate is a nonspecific marker of stress/pain and does not directly reflect renal perfusion or tubular injury risk once intra/post-op hemodynamics are accounted for.
Use of a PA catheter is a proxy for higher surgical/ICU acuity and anticipated hemodynamic instability, which can relate to AKI risk, but it is not a physiologic driver itself.

Peak core temperature may reflect inflammatory response or infection risk, but perioperative temperature extremes are not a primary established predictor of post-cardiac surgery AKI compared with perfusion/pressure variables.

Inhaled nitric oxide use suggests pulmonary hypertension/RV strain and potential low cardiac output states that can impair renal perfusion, but it is an indirect proxy rather than a direct AKI marker.
Large crystalloid volumes can indicate bleeding/vasoplegia and contribute to venous congestion/hemodilution, which may worsen renal function, but volume given is confounded by case complexity.

Synthetic colloids (depending on agent) have been associated with AKI risk and are often used in sicker patients; still, intraop dosing is a proxy and may be collinear with overall resuscitation intensity.
Albumin use reflects volume resuscitation strategy and oncotic support; it may correlate with hemodynamic instability but is not a direct nephrotoxic exposure or definitive AKI predictor.
Intraoperative hypoglycemia/low glucose is not a typical direct driver of AKI; glycemic control relates more to overall illness severity than renal-specific injury mechanisms.

Intraoperative vasodilator use can signal hypertension management or afterload reduction; it may contribute to hypotension episodes affecting renal perfusion, but the relationship is indirect and confounded.
Intra-procedural EEG monitoring reflects neurologic monitoring needs and case complexity, with no specific mechanistic link to postoperative creatinine rise.
Pre-incision TEE is routine in many cardiac surgeries and mainly reflects standard monitoring rather than renal perfusion risk.
Reduced LVEF is an established risk factor for low cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion after cardiac surgery, increasing AKI risk.
RV dysfunction predisposes to elevated venous pressures and renal venous congestion with reduced effective renal perfusion, an established contributor to AKI.
Significant MR can reflect chronic heart failure physiology and perioperative hemodynamic instability, but its association with AKI is indirect and mediated through cardiac output/pressures.
Mitral stenosis may contribute to pulmonary hypertension and right-sided strain, but it is not a primary established predictor of postoperative AKI compared with direct hemodynamic measures.
Aortic regurgitation can affect perioperative hemodynamics, yet its link to AKI is indirect and typically weaker than global ventricular function or shock markers.
Significant valvular disease can predispose to perioperative low cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion, but it is an indirect and heterogeneous predictor once postoperative hemodynamics are known.
Whether aortic valve area was assessed reflects documentation/testing rather than a physiologic insult; it is not a direct AKI driver.

Tricuspid regurgitation can indicate right-sided dysfunction and venous congestion, which can worsen renal perfusion pressure, but it remains an indirect predictor compared with postoperative CVP/pressors/urine output.
Patent foramen ovale has no meaningful direct relationship to postoperative renal injury risk.
Assessment of the ascending aorta is a procedural/documentation variable and does not itself reflect renal perfusion or nephrotoxic exposure.
Aortic size relates to surgical complexity but is not an established independent predictor of AKI compared with bypass time, hemodynamics, and renal labs.
Aortic atherosclerosis may correlate with embolic burden and vascular disease, which can contribute to renal ischemia, but evidence is indirect for predicting creatinine rise.
Mobile atheroma increases risk of embolization during manipulation/CPB, plausibly including renal microembolization, but it is not a definitive AKI marker.
Whether the arch was visualized is a workflow/documentation feature and not a physiologic determinant of postoperative creatinine change.
Arch atheroma burden may reflect systemic atherosclerosis and embolic risk, which can contribute to renal injury, but the link is indirect.
Mobile arch atheroma suggests higher embolic potential during surgery, which can contribute to renal ischemic injury, though it remains a secondary predictor.
Use of cardiopulmonary bypass is an established AKI risk factor via inflammation, hemolysis, nonpulsatile flow, and renal hypoperfusion; it is a key perioperative exposure.
Autologous priming/retrograde autologous priming may reduce hemodilution and transfusion needs, potentially affecting AKI risk, but effects are modest and context-dependent.
Higher intraoperative crystalloid can reflect hemodilution, capillary leak, and fluid overload, which may worsen renal congestion and AKI risk, but it is a nonspecific proxy for case complexity.
Synthetic colloids (e.g., HES) are associated with AKI risk in critical illness and may contribute to renal tubular injury; intraoperative exposure is clinically relevant if present.
Albumin use reflects volume management and oncotic support; it may correlate with hemodynamic instability but is not a strong independent driver of AKI compared with perfusion and vasopressor needs.

Need for hemofiltration/perfusion support reflects severe perioperative renal dysfunction or fluid overload and is strongly associated with subsequent creatinine rise. It is a near-direct marker of early AKI severity/trajectory.
Difficulty weaning inotropes off CPB suggests low cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion risk, an established AKI mechanism. However it is indirect and can be transient immediately post-bypass.
High vasopressor requirement to wean from CPB indicates vasoplegia/shock physiology and impaired renal perfusion pressure, increasing AKI risk. Still an indirect proxy rather than a renal biomarker.
Having a post-TEE is largely procedural/monitoring practice and does not directly quantify renal perfusion or injury. Any association is likely confounded by case complexity.
SAM can cause dynamic LVOT obstruction and hypotension, which could reduce renal perfusion. It is relatively uncommon and an indirect, situational contributor to AKI risk.
Return-to-CPB or CPB-related echo assessment reflects intraoperative instability/complexity that may correlate with AKI risk. It is an indirect proxy and not specific for renal injury.
Lower LVEF is an established risk factor for postoperative AKI via low cardiac output and venous congestion. Post-incision estimate is indirect and may not reflect postoperative hemodynamics.

RV dysfunction can drive venous congestion and elevated renal venous pressure, a recognized pathway to AKI after cardiac surgery. It is a meaningful hemodynamic risk factor though not definitive alone.
Intraoperative arrhythmias can cause hypotension/low output episodes and renal hypoperfusion. Association is plausible but heterogeneous and often transient.

Postoperative hypothermia/rewarming relates to systemic stress and vasoconstriction but is not a primary driver of AKI compared with perfusion and congestion variables. Likely weak, nonspecific signal.

Elevated INR may reflect hepatic hypoperfusion, CPB-related coagulopathy, or massive transfusion—markers of severe illness that correlate with AKI risk. It is indirect and confounded by anticoagulation practices.

Leukocytosis can indicate inflammation/infection and overall physiologic stress, which may contribute to AKI risk. It is nonspecific and weakly predictive compared with hemodynamics and renal markers.
Thrombocytopenia after CPB can reflect systemic inflammation/consumption and severity of illness, which correlates with AKI risk. It is indirect and not kidney-specific.
Low hematocrit/anemia reduces oxygen delivery and is associated with postoperative AKI, especially after CPB and transfusion-heavy courses. It is an established but moderate-strength risk factor.
Low fibrinogen suggests bleeding/consumption and severe operative stress, which can correlate with AKI through shock/transfusion pathways. It is indirect and not specific for renal injury.

Elevated lactate is a strong marker of global hypoperfusion/low cardiac output and predicts organ dysfunction including AKI after cardiac surgery. It captures severity of shock physiology more directly than many other labs.

Postoperative propofol exposure is not a direct driver of AKI; any association would be indirect via hypotension or illness severity. In a sparse linear model it is likely redundant with hemodynamic variables.
Pain score on POD3 is temporally downstream/late relative to the 36h feature window and is not a physiologic mechanism for AKI. It may weakly reflect overall recovery but is nonspecific.

Smoking is associated with vascular disease and perioperative pulmonary complications that can indirectly worsen renal perfusion. However it is not a strong short-term predictor of creatinine rise after cardiac surgery compared with hemodynamics and renal labs.

Former smoking has a weaker and more heterogeneous relationship to acute postoperative AKI than current smoking. Any effect is largely mediated through comorbid vascular disease already captured elsewhere.
Atrial fibrillation can contribute to perioperative hemodynamic instability and low cardiac output episodes that predispose to AKI. Paroxysmal AF is a modest risk marker but not a direct biomarker.

Persistent AF more strongly reflects chronic atrial/ventricular dysfunction and risk of postoperative low output and congestion, which can impair renal perfusion. Still an established risk factor rather than a direct renal marker.
Antegrade cardioplegia delivery technique has no clear direct mechanistic link to renal injury. Any association would be confounded by procedure type/complexity.

Retrograde cardioplegia is primarily a surgical technique choice and is not a direct determinant of postoperative renal function. Potential links are indirect via operative complexity and bypass time.
Blood vs crystalloid cardioplegia has limited and inconsistent direct association with postoperative AKI compared with perfusion pressure, bypass duration, and shock. Treat as weak/indirect at most.
Crystalloid cardioplegia choice is not a direct renal insult and is largely a procedural preference. Any signal is likely confounded by case mix and operative factors.

Acute heart failure around surgery increases risk of renal hypoperfusion and venous congestion (cardiorenal syndrome), both key pathways to AKI. It is an established perioperative risk factor for creatinine rise.

Chronic heart failure predisposes to low effective arterial blood volume and renal venous congestion, increasing susceptibility to postoperative AKI. It is a well-known baseline risk factor but not definitive alone.

Systolic dysfunction is closely tied to low cardiac output states and need for vasoactive support, which are strongly linked to AKI after cardiac surgery. This is an established risk factor for subsequent creatinine increase.

Diastolic dysfunction can cause elevated filling pressures and congestion that impair renal function, but the relationship to AKI is generally weaker than systolic failure. Consider as plausible-to-established but not a direct predictor.

Early mean SpO2 in the immediate postoperative period is often transiently affected by ventilation/anesthesia and is a nonspecific marker for AKI. Hypoxemia can contribute to renal ischemia, but mean values in 0–12h are conservative and capped.

Persistently lower mean SpO2 in 13–24h may reflect ongoing respiratory failure and systemic hypoxia that can worsen renal injury. Still indirect and less informative than hemodynamics/renal labs, so kept low.

Sustained oxygenation may reflect overall cardiopulmonary stability, but mean SpO2 is a nonspecific and often artifact-prone proxy for renal perfusion. Extremes (hypoxemia episodes) are more mechanistically linked to AKI than averages.
High SpO2 is not a plausible driver of AKI and mainly reflects supplemental oxygen use. Early post-op values are heavily influenced by ventilation/FiO2 and are weakly informative for renal injury.
Maximum SpO2 largely reflects oxygen therapy rather than renal-relevant physiology. Provides little incremental signal for AKI risk.
Maximum SpO2 is not a marker of hypoxic insult and is minimally related to kidney injury. It is mostly determined by oxygen delivery settings.

Hypoxemia episodes can worsen renal medullary oxygenation and correlate with hemodynamic/respiratory instability, plausibly increasing AKI risk. In the immediate 0–12h post-op window, transient derangements are common, so the score is capped conservatively.
Persistent or recurrent hypoxemia in the trajectory phase suggests ongoing instability and can contribute to renal ischemic stress. More informative than early post-op but still indirect for AKI.

Late hypoxemia close to the outcome window is a stronger leading indicator of systemic compromise and reduced renal oxygen delivery. While not kidney-specific, it can meaningfully track risk of subsequent creatinine rise.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity and routine ICU practice rather than a renal mechanism. Early post-op continuous monitoring makes this a weak behavioral proxy.
SpO2 measurement frequency is largely protocol-driven and not specific to AKI suspicion. Adds little beyond the physiologic values themselves.
Continued frequent SpO2 checks may reflect acuity but is nonspecific and highly confounded by ventilation status. Kept low per behavioral-proxy rule.

Mean PAP reflects RV afterload and cardiopulmonary status, which can indirectly affect renal perfusion via low cardiac output/venous congestion. In the immediate post-op period it is often transiently abnormal and less predictive.

Ongoing elevation in mean PAP may indicate RV dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension contributing to low forward flow and renal hypoperfusion. Still indirect and collinear with more informative extremes.

Later sustained elevation in mean PAP can track persistent RV strain and systemic congestion that can worsen renal function. However, extremes are typically more reflective of acute hemodynamic insults than averages.

Acute spikes in mean PAP can signal RV failure, hypoxia/hypercapnia, or pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to reduced cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion. In 0–12h, abnormalities are common post-CPB so the score is conservatively capped.

Maximal PAP elevations during 13–24h suggest ongoing RV afterload crises and hemodynamic instability, which are established contributors to AKI risk. More informative than the mean due to capturing acute insults.

Late PAP spikes close to hour 60 can indicate persistent or worsening RV dysfunction and venous congestion/low output, both strongly linked to postoperative AKI. This extreme aggregation is preferred over mean to reduce collinearity and better capture pathologic episodes.

Low PA pressure can reflect low preload/low output states that may reduce renal perfusion, but early post-op values are often transient and treatment-driven. Also a less direct AKI driver than systemic perfusion pressure or venous congestion.
Persistently low PA pressures in the trajectory phase can indicate ongoing low filling/low output physiology affecting renal perfusion. Still indirect and collinear with other hemodynamic markers.

In the leading-indicator window, low PA pressures may signal sustained low preload/low cardiac output contributing to renal hypoperfusion. Remains an indirect proxy compared with direct cardiac output/MAP measures.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity (e.g., PA catheter presence/acuity) rather than a physiologic mechanism of AKI. Early post-op monitoring is common and not specific.
More frequent PA pressure documentation may indicate ongoing shock/instability prompting closer monitoring, which correlates with AKI risk. Still a behavioral proxy and non-specific.

Continued frequent PA pressure measurements late may reflect persistent hemodynamic concern (e.g., low output/right heart failure) associated with AKI. Nonetheless it is not a direct physiologic marker.
Frequency of cardiac index measurement reflects device use/acuity rather than renal physiology. In the immediate post-op period, continuous monitoring is routine and weakly discriminative.
Ongoing continuous CI monitoring can indicate persistent instability/need for titration of inotropes, which is associated with AKI risk. Still a proxy variable and should remain low.
Continued CI monitoring close to outcome may signal unresolved low-output state or shock management, both linked to AKI. However, it is measurement behavior rather than a direct insult.

Elevated mean CVP reflects venous congestion and reduced renal perfusion gradient, a recognized AKI mechanism after cardiac surgery. In the first 12h it is often influenced by ventilation/fluids and transient.
Sustained venous congestion during 13–24h is more prognostic for cardiorenal syndrome and postoperative AKI than immediate post-op values. Mean CVP captures ongoing congestion burden.

Persistently high CVP in the 25–36h window is a strong indicator of venous congestion/right heart dysfunction, reducing renal perfusion pressure and strongly associating with AKI. This is a clinically meaningful hemodynamic driver close to the 60h creatinine outcome.

Peak CVP can capture acute congestion episodes that may impair renal perfusion, but early post-op spikes are common with ventilator changes and fluid resuscitation. To limit collinearity with mean CVP, keep modest.
Higher CVP maxima in the trajectory phase may reflect episodic severe congestion/right ventricular failure, which is linked to AKI. Max adds some value beyond mean by capturing worst congestion.

Severe CVP elevations close to outcome suggest significant venous congestion and impaired renal perfusion gradient, a strong postoperative AKI predictor. Max captures the worst hemodynamic insult in the most relevant window.

Low CVP minima are less specific for AKI and often reflect transient underfilling or measurement/ventilator effects early after surgery. Also largely redundant with other perfusion markers and fluid management variables.

Low CVP can reflect relative hypovolemia/low preload and reduced renal perfusion during the trajectory phase, which can contribute to AKI risk. Capped below stronger late-window hemodynamic indicators.

Persistently low CVP closer to the outcome can indicate ongoing underfilling/low effective circulating volume and impaired renal perfusion, increasing AKI risk. The minimum captures acute under-resuscitation better than mean/measured.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity immediately post-op rather than a renal mechanism. Early post-bypass period is highly protocolized, limiting prognostic specificity.
More frequent CVP checks may reflect clinician concern for hemodynamic instability, indirectly related to AKI risk. Still primarily a behavior/acuity proxy and kept <0.05.
Increased CVP monitoring late may indicate ongoing shock/volume management complexity, which correlates with AKI risk. As a behavioral proxy (not physiology), it remains <0.05.

Average FiO2 in the immediate post-op window is heavily influenced by routine ventilator weaning practices and does not directly reflect renal perfusion. Any association with AKI is indirect via illness severity.

Sustained higher oxygen requirement can indicate cardiopulmonary dysfunction and overall severity, indirectly increasing AKI risk. Mean is less informative than extremes for acute insults, so kept low.

Ongoing elevated FiO2 requirement closer to hour 60 suggests persistent respiratory/cardiac failure and higher systemic illness burden associated with AKI. Still an indirect marker and not kidney-specific.

A high FiO2 maximum early may reflect transient post-op hypoxemia or hemodynamic instability, indirectly linked to AKI via shock/hypoxia. Conservative scoring due to common transient derangements in 0–12h.
A high FiO2 spike during 13–24h can signal worsening pulmonary edema/low cardiac output states that correlate with AKI risk. Max better captures acute deterioration than mean, but remains indirect.

Late high FiO2 peaks suggest significant cardiopulmonary compromise near the outcome window, which is associated with renal hypoperfusion and AKI. Kept at the indirect-link cap because FiO2 is not a renal biomarker.
Minimum FiO2 largely reflects ventilator weaning targets and may be low even in sick patients once stabilized. It has weak mechanistic linkage to AKI.
Lower minimum FiO2 generally indicates better respiratory status and is not a direct driver of AKI. Limited prognostic value compared with maxima or hemodynamic variables.
Minimum FiO2 late may weakly reflect overall recovery vs persistent respiratory failure, but it is not kidney-specific. Any association with creatinine rise is indirect and small.
Frequency of FiO2 documentation is largely protocol-driven in the immediate post-op period and reflects charting/monitoring rather than AKI physiology. Therefore minimal predictive value.
More frequent FiO2 recording may reflect ventilatory instability or clinician attention, indirectly associated with severity of illness. As a behavioral proxy, it is kept well below 0.05.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects clinician concern/acuity rather than a direct renal mechanism. Higher monitoring may correlate with overall instability, but is nonspecific for AKI.

Early post-op ventilator rate settings are largely protocolized and reflect respiratory management more than renal perfusion. Mean values also smooth transient events and add collinearity with extremes.

Persistently higher set rates can be a proxy for ongoing respiratory failure/acidosis and illness severity, indirectly linked to AKI risk. Mean aggregation is still nonspecific and collinear with max/min.

A high maximum set rate may indicate acute hypercapnia/acidosis management or severe lung dysfunction, which can accompany hemodynamic stress. In the immediate 0–12h window this is often transient, so weight is conservative.

A higher max set rate in 13–24h suggests failure to stabilize and possible ongoing acidosis/respiratory distress, indirectly associated with AKI via severity and catecholamine exposure. Still not a direct renal predictor.
Low minimum set rate is usually driven by sedation/weaning strategy and is not a recognized trigger for AKI. In 0–12h it is heavily influenced by routine post-op ventilation practices.
Minimum set rate mainly reflects ventilator strategy rather than renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity. It provides little specific prognostic information for creatinine rise.
Measurement frequency is a behavioral proxy and not a physiologic driver of AKI. In the immediate post-op period, frequent documentation is routine and poorly discriminative.
More frequent recording may reflect ICU intensity but is nonspecific for renal injury. It should be kept low to avoid over-weighting documentation patterns.

Increased measurement frequency closer to outcome may indicate ongoing instability or ventilator adjustments, indirectly associated with AKI risk. Still primarily a clinician-behavior signal, not a renal biomarker.
Mean set tidal volume early post-op is protocol-driven (lung-protective ventilation) and not directly linked to renal perfusion. Mean aggregation is also redundant with max values.

Persistently higher tidal volumes can reflect ventilatory strategy and lung mechanics, indirectly tied to systemic inflammation and severity. However, it remains a weak and nonspecific predictor for AKI.

Later sustained tidal volume settings may reflect ongoing respiratory failure or reduced lung compliance, correlating with overall critical illness that predisposes to AKI. Still indirect and not kidney-specific.

A high maximum tidal volume may indicate episodes of non–lung-protective ventilation or ventilator dyssynchrony, which can contribute to inflammation and hemodynamic effects. In 0–12h this is often transient and protocol-related.

Higher max tidal volumes in 13–24h may signal ongoing difficult ventilation and systemic stress, indirectly increasing AKI risk. Max is preferred over mean to capture potentially injurious extremes while limiting collinearity.

In the 25–36h leading window, high maximum tidal volumes may reflect persistent severe respiratory mechanics or dyssynchrony with greater systemic inflammation and hemodynamic compromise, indirectly associated with AKI. Still not a direct renal biomarker, so capped at plausible-indirect strength.

Set tidal volume is not a direct driver of postoperative AKI; any association is indirect via lung mechanics and hemodynamics. Using the minimum set value adds little physiologic specificity for renal perfusion risk in this early, highly protocol-driven window.
Minimum set tidal volume mainly reflects ventilator strategy rather than renal injury biology. Any link to AKI would be mediated and weak compared with direct hemodynamic/renal markers.

Persistently low set tidal volumes may reflect ongoing respiratory failure/ARDS severity, which can correlate with multi-organ dysfunction and AKI risk. Still indirect and largely protocolized, so kept low for sparsity.
Measurement frequency is a documentation/acuity proxy rather than a physiologic mechanism for AKI. In the immediate post-op period it is routine and not specific for impending renal dysfunction.
How often tidal volume is recorded reflects workflow and ventilator management intensity, not kidney perfusion or nephrotoxicity. Weak and nonspecific for AKI prediction.
More frequent ventilator adjustments/recording may indicate instability, which can co-occur with AKI, but remains an indirect behavioral signal. Capped low per measured-feature rule.

Higher mean PEEP can reduce venous return and cardiac output, potentially lowering renal perfusion, but early post-op PEEP is often standardized and transient. Mean is also less sensitive than extremes for acute hemodynamic insult.

Sustained higher PEEP during the trajectory phase may reflect ongoing hypoxemia/ARDS and can impair renal perfusion via reduced preload and increased intrathoracic pressure. Still indirect and averaged, so modest.

Persistently elevated mean PEEP closer to the outcome can indicate significant respiratory failure and sustained hemodynamic compromise that increases AKI risk. Mean is less specific than max, so kept at the plausible/indirect cap.

A high PEEP maximum can mark an acute episode of severe hypoxemia or aggressive ventilatory support that may transiently reduce renal perfusion. Early post-op derangements are common, so conservatively scored within the 0_12h cap.

Higher PEEP maxima in this phase suggest worsening lung mechanics/hypoxemia and potential hemodynamic compromise, both associated with AKI in ICU patients. Extremes better capture acute insult than mean, so prioritized.

High PEEP maxima late (25–36h) can indicate severe ongoing respiratory failure requiring high intrathoracic pressures, which can reduce cardiac output and renal blood flow. As an extreme close to the outcome, it is a stronger indirect predictor of AKI.
Minimum PEEP is usually set by protocol (e.g., 5 cmH2O) and does not capture the pathologic episodes relevant to renal hypoperfusion. Provides little incremental AKI signal versus max.
Low minimum PEEP is not a recognized trigger for AKI and is often a default setting. It is also collinear with other PEEP summaries and less informative than maxima.
Minimum PEEP remains largely protocol-driven and does not reflect acute hemodynamic stressors that drive AKI. Kept minimal to avoid redundancy with more informative PEEP max features.
Frequency of PEEP documentation is a care-process marker and not a physiologic determinant of AKI. In the immediate post-op period it is routine and nonspecific for renal injury risk.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects clinician attention/acuity rather than a direct renal mechanism. Ventilator monitoring intensity is not a specific predictor of AKI.
More frequent PEEP documentation may proxy ongoing respiratory failure/instability, which can correlate with shock and AKI risk, but it is indirect. As a _measured feature it remains capped low.
Average plateau pressure early post-op is a nonspecific marker of lung mechanics and ventilator strategy. Early (0–12h) values are often transient and weakly linked to renal hypoperfusion.

Sustained higher plateau pressures can reflect worse lung compliance and higher intrathoracic pressures that may reduce venous return/renal perfusion, but the mean is less informative than extremes. Kept low to avoid collinearity with max/min.

Peak plateau pressures can indicate acute high intrathoracic pressure episodes that may impair cardiac output and renal perfusion. In the immediate 0–12h period this is common and transient, so conservatively scored.

Persistently high peak plateau pressures in the trajectory phase suggest ongoing poor compliance/ARDS physiology and higher intrathoracic pressures, which can contribute to reduced renal perfusion and AKI. Max is preferred over mean for capturing injurious episodes.
Minimum plateau pressure is not a plausible trigger for AKI and mostly reflects periods of lower ventilatory stress. Provides little incremental prognostic information.
Low plateau pressures are not mechanistically linked to AKI and are generally reassuring rather than harmful. Minimal expected predictive value.
Frequency of plateau pressure measurement reflects monitoring practice rather than renal physiology. Early post-op ventilator checks are routine and not AKI-specific.
More frequent plateau pressure checks may indicate ventilatory difficulty, but remains an indirect behavioral proxy. Not specific enough to warrant higher inclusion.

Increased measurement frequency late may reflect persistent respiratory failure and higher overall illness severity, which correlates with AKI risk. Still capped because it is not a physiologic exposure.
Mean minute ventilation early post-op is influenced by sedation, temperature, and ventilator settings and is not a direct AKI driver. Early derangements are often transient.

Higher sustained minute ventilation can reflect metabolic acidosis/sepsis or increased dead space, which may correlate with shock and AKI, but it is indirect. Mean is less informative than extremes for acute insults.

High peak minute ventilation may signal acute metabolic acidosis or ventilatory stress, which can accompany hypoperfusion states associated with AKI. In 0–12h it is common post-op, so conservatively scored.

Peak minute ventilation in 13–24h may indicate evolving metabolic acidosis (e.g., lactic acidosis) or worsening lung disease, both associated with higher AKI risk via systemic illness/shock. Max is preferred over mean to capture clinically significant episodes.
Low minimum minute ventilation usually reflects sedation/controlled ventilation rather than a renal insult. Not a plausible direct predictor of creatinine rise.

Low minute ventilation can reflect hypoventilation, sedation, or evolving respiratory failure, which may correlate with overall severity and renal hypoperfusion. As an indirect marker (and using a minimum), it has limited specificity for AKI.

Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity rather than a physiologic mechanism for AKI. Early (0–12h) ordering is routine post-cardiac surgery and is not specific for impending renal injury.
More frequent documentation may indicate ongoing instability or ventilator dependence, indirectly associated with AKI risk. Still primarily a behavioral/acuity proxy and not a direct renal predictor.

Persistent need for frequent ventilatory assessments late (25–36h) can signal ongoing critical illness and higher AKI risk. However, it remains a monitoring-intensity proxy rather than a causal renal marker.

Average oxygen device level in the immediate postoperative window is heavily influenced by routine extubation/weaning practices and is not specific for renal hypoperfusion. Mean aggregation further dilutes acute insults relevant to AKI.
Higher average oxygen support may reflect persistent cardiopulmonary dysfunction and illness severity, indirectly linked to AKI. Mean device level is still a nonspecific surrogate.

Sustained higher oxygen device requirements closer to outcome can indicate ongoing heart/lung failure and systemic hypoxia, which can worsen renal perfusion. As a mean and device-coded variable, it remains indirect.

Maximum oxygen device requirement captures acute respiratory compromise, which can accompany low cardiac output or shock states that predispose to AKI. In 0–12h this is often transient post-op, so importance is conservative.

A high maximum oxygen device requirement during 13–24h suggests failure to stabilize and greater severity of illness, which is associated with AKI. Max better captures episodic decompensation than mean/min, so it is preferred among device aggregations.

Late high oxygen device requirement (max) is a leading indicator of persistent cardiopulmonary failure and systemic hypoxemia, both associated with renal ischemia and AKI. Max is the most informative aggregation for acute deterioration.
Minimum oxygen device requirement mainly reflects periods of stability or weaning and is not a trigger for AKI. In the immediate post-op window it is strongly protocol-driven.

Minimum device level is a weak indicator of physiologic stress and is less informative than maxima for capturing decompensation relevant to AKI. It adds collinearity with other device summaries without clear added value.
Minimum oxygen device requirement late is more reflective of best-case respiratory status than renal risk. It is unlikely to add predictive value beyond max/mean and is capped to reduce redundancy.
Frequency of documenting oxygen device is largely workflow-related and routine immediately after surgery. It is not a physiologic mechanism for AKI and is not specific for renal risk.

More frequent respiratory therapy documentation may indicate ongoing respiratory instability and higher overall acuity, indirectly associated with AKI. Still primarily a behavioral proxy and thus kept low.

Late frequent oxygen device assessments can reflect persistent respiratory failure and critical illness, which correlates with AKI risk. As a measurement-frequency feature, it remains nonspecific and is kept <0.05.

Average chest tube output is an indirect marker of bleeding/transfusion and hemodynamic stress, but the mean blunts acute hemorrhage signals. Early (0–12h) values are often transient post-op, so predictive value for later AKI is limited.

Persistently higher average drainage may reflect ongoing bleeding/inflammation and need for blood products, which can contribute to AKI risk indirectly. Mean aggregation is still less informative than extremes for acute insult.

Ongoing average chest tube output closer to the outcome may indicate continued bleeding or coagulopathy with downstream renal hypoperfusion risk. Still an indirect signal and less specific than hemodynamics/renal labs.

Peak early chest tube output can capture acute hemorrhage leading to hypotension, transfusion, and renal hypoperfusion. Capped by the 0–12h epoch maximum and because bleeding is an indirect (not renal-specific) driver.

A high maximum output in 13–24h suggests ongoing bleeding/tamponade physiology risk and potential low-flow states that predispose to AKI. This is more informative than the mean because it captures acute episodes.

Late peak drainage (25–36h) is a leading indicator of continued bleeding or instability, increasing likelihood of renal hypoperfusion and transfusion-associated kidney injury. Max best captures clinically meaningful acute events.
Minimum chest tube output is rarely a direct AKI predictor and may reflect routine low drainage rather than pathology. Low output can be due to tube position/clot and is nonspecific for renal risk.
Minimum drainage remains nonspecific and is more influenced by measurement/tube factors than systemic perfusion. It provides little incremental information for AKI prediction.
Low minimum output is not a reliable marker of hemodynamic compromise and is not mechanistically linked to AKI. Any association would be weak and confounded by tube function.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects nursing/ICU workflow rather than physiology, especially immediately post-op when monitoring is routine. It is not a direct mechanism for AKI.
More frequent documentation may weakly proxy concern for bleeding/instability, which can relate to AKI risk indirectly. Still primarily a behavioral/acuity marker and should remain low.
Increased measurement frequency late may indicate ongoing concern for bleeding or deterioration, indirectly associated with AKI. As a behavioral proxy, it should be kept low.

Mean PAP reflects pulmonary hypertension/RV afterload and can correlate with low cardiac output and venous congestion affecting renal perfusion. In the immediate 0–12h period, values are often influenced by ventilation/CPB effects, so conservatively scored.

Sustained elevated PAP in 13–24h may indicate RV dysfunction and systemic venous congestion, which is associated with AKI after cardiac surgery. Mean is less sensitive than extremes but can reflect persistent physiology.

Persistently high PAP closer to hour 60 can signal ongoing RV failure/venous congestion and reduced effective renal perfusion pressure, a recognized AKI pathway. Mean may capture sustained congestion relevant to kidney injury.

A high peak PAP early can reflect acute RV strain, hypoxia/hypercapnia, or pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to low forward flow and renal hypoperfusion. Scored higher than mean because extremes better capture acute hemodynamic insult, but capped by the 0–12h epoch limit.

Elevated PAP systolic can reflect RV strain/volume overload and venous congestion, which can contribute to AKI, but it is indirect and often collinear with other hemodynamic markers. In the 13–24h epoch, treat as a modest trajectory signal.

Persistently high PAP systolic closer to the outcome may indicate ongoing RV dysfunction and systemic venous congestion, plausibly worsening renal perfusion. Still an indirect marker and likely redundant with CVP/echo/vasopressor variables, so kept low.

Low PAP systolic may reflect low pulmonary flow/low cardiac output states that can reduce renal perfusion, but immediate post-op values are often transient and treatment-related. Conservative scoring due to early epoch and indirectness.
A low PAP systolic in this window can be a proxy for low cardiac output or hypovolemia, both associated with AKI risk. Still nonspecific and collinear with MAP/CI/vasopressor needs.

Low PAP systolic late (25–36h) may indicate persistent low flow/low output physiology, a more relevant leading indicator for subsequent creatinine rise. Remains indirect, so not scored as a strong predictor.

Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity (e.g., PA catheter presence/acuity) rather than a renal mechanism. Early post-op monitoring is routine, so it adds little specific AKI signal.
More frequent PAP documentation may indicate ongoing hemodynamic instability, but it is a behavioral proxy and highly confounded by device use and staffing. Kept below 0.05 per rule.
Continued frequent PAP measurements late may reflect persistent shock/instability prompting closer monitoring, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still a proxy variable and not a physiologic driver.

Mean PAP diastolic in the immediate post-op period is heavily influenced by transient ventilator/PEEP and volume shifts and is not a direct AKI driver. Also likely redundant with extremes and other hemodynamics.

Sustained higher PAP diastolic can suggest elevated pulmonary vascular resistance or left-sided filling pressures, indirectly relating to congestion and AKI. Mean aggregation is less sensitive to acute insults than extremes, so kept low.

A persistently elevated PAP diastolic closer to hour 60 may reflect ongoing congestion/RV afterload that can impair renal function via venous congestion. Mean is still less informative than max/min for acute physiology, limiting importance.

High PAP diastolic peaks can indicate acute pulmonary hypertension/left-sided congestion and potential RV strain, indirectly contributing to renal venous congestion. Early epoch values are often transient post-bypass, so conservative.

Peak PAP diastolic in 13–24h may better capture clinically meaningful congestion or rising pulmonary pressures than the mean. This can be associated with worse renal outcomes via venous congestion, but remains indirect.

Late peaks in PAP diastolic may signal persistent/worsening congestion or RV dysfunction near the outcome window, which is plausibly linked to AKI through renal venous hypertension and reduced perfusion gradient. Chosen over mean to reduce collinearity and capture extremes.

Low PAP diastolic minima early post-op are nonspecific and often reflect transient low preload or ventilator effects rather than sustained renal hypoperfusion. Limited incremental AKI information in this epoch.

Low PAP diastolic minima may reflect low preload/low flow states that can contribute to renal hypoperfusion, but it is nonspecific and collinear with other shock markers. Moderate-low importance given trajectory window.

Low diastolic pulmonary artery pressure can reflect low RV preload/forward flow or vasodilatory shock, which may reduce renal perfusion and contribute to AKI. As an indirect hemodynamic marker (and less direct than MAP/CO), keep moderate weight.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity rather than renal physiology. Early post-op ordering is routine in many CTICU patients and is not specific for impending AKI.
Counts of measurements are a behavioral proxy for acuity and are not a direct mechanism for AKI. Continued PAP monitoring may reflect severity but is nonspecific.
More frequent PAP measurements late may indicate hemodynamic instability, which can correlate with AKI risk, but it remains an indirect clinician-behavior signal. Kept <0.05 per rules.

Average heart rate in the immediate post-op window is often influenced by pain, pacing, and inotropes and is weakly specific for renal hypoperfusion. Mean is also less informative than extremes for acute insults.
Sustained tachycardia can reflect ongoing shock, low stroke volume, or sepsis physiology that may predispose to AKI, but mean HR is still nonspecific. Capped low to avoid redundancy with max/min.
Persistently elevated or depressed mean pulse closer to the outcome can indicate ongoing hemodynamic stress affecting renal perfusion. Still indirect and less informative than extremes, so kept low.

Early extreme tachycardia may signal bleeding, pain/agitation, or low cardiac output states that can reduce renal perfusion, but this period is highly transient post-op. Conservative scoring per 0–12h cap.
Max pulse during the trajectory phase can capture episodes of instability (e.g., shock/arrhythmia) that may contribute to renal ischemia. More informative than mean, but still indirect.

Late episodes of marked tachycardia can reflect ongoing low output, sepsis, or arrhythmia burden, all associated with AKI risk via impaired renal perfusion. Max captures acute insults better than mean.

Bradycardia early post-op is often pacing/medication related and not specific for renal injury, though severe bradycardia could reduce cardiac output. Conservative scoring given immediate post-op confounding.
Low minimum pulse may capture clinically significant bradyarrhythmias or excessive beta-blockade/pacing issues that can reduce renal perfusion. Still an indirect marker, so kept modest.
Late bradycardic episodes closer to hour 60 may indicate conduction issues or low-output physiology that can impair renal blood flow. Minimum is more informative than mean for capturing these events.
Pulse measurement frequency reflects monitoring practices (often continuous) rather than a causal pathway to AKI. Not specific for renal risk.
Measurement count is a weak behavioral proxy and provides little incremental physiologic information for AKI prediction. Kept minimal to enforce sparsity.
Even late, pulse measurement frequency is largely driven by ICU workflow and monitoring rather than renal pathophysiology. Not a specific predictor of creatinine rise.

Average inspired O2 concentration is not a direct driver of AKI and is heavily confounded by routine ventilator management early post-op. Any signal is indirect via illness severity and oxygenation strategy.

High FiO2 peaks can reflect acute hypoxemia/hemodynamic instability, which may contribute to renal hypoxia, but this is nonspecific. In the immediate 0–12h window it is often transient and protocol-driven.
Low FiO2 minima usually reflect weaning rather than renal risk and has no clear mechanistic link to AKI. Early post-op values are dominated by ventilator practice patterns.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity and workflow rather than renal physiology. It is not a specific indicator of impending AKI.
O2 documentation frequency is a behavioral/acuity proxy and not a mechanistic AKI predictor. Any association would be weak and confounded by overall instability.

More frequent O2 recording late may indicate ongoing respiratory/hemodynamic instability, indirectly increasing AKI risk, but it remains nonspecific. Kept low because it is a monitoring artifact rather than physiology.

Nitrous oxide exposure is not an established contributor to postoperative AKI compared with hemodynamics, nephrotoxins, and perfusion. Early post-op use is uncommon and likely reflects anesthesia practice rather than renal risk.
Peak N2O concentration has no strong evidence linking it to renal hypoperfusion or tubular injury in this context. Any signal would be indirect and highly practice-dependent.
Minimum N2O is clinically uninformative for AKI risk and largely reflects whether the agent was used. No plausible direct renal mechanism.
Frequency of N2O documentation is a workflow artifact and not a physiologic marker of renal injury. Unlikely to add predictive value beyond other severity indicators.
N2O measurement frequency is not a recognized AKI risk factor and mainly reflects anesthesia/ventilator documentation patterns. Association with creatinine rise would be weak and confounded.
Late N2O measurement is rare and would reflect practice rather than renal pathophysiology. Not expected to meaningfully predict creatinine_ratio.
Mean delivered medical air fraction is essentially the complement of FiO2 and does not directly relate to renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity. Early post-op values are protocol-driven.
High air fraction (lower FiO2) peaks are not a known trigger for AKI and mostly reflect ventilator settings. Any relationship to renal outcomes would be indirect and weak.
Low air fraction (higher FiO2) minima duplicates FiO2 extremes and adds collinearity without clearer renal mechanism. Capped low to avoid redundancy.
Air documentation frequency is a monitoring artifact and not a physiologic predictor of AKI. It is unlikely to capture clinician concern specific to renal injury.
Measurement frequency of delivered air is a documentation/monitoring artifact and not a physiologic driver of AKI. At most it weakly proxies acuity/ventilation complexity.
Still primarily a monitoring/behavioral proxy rather than a renal mechanism. Slightly higher only because later-epoch care intensity can correlate with evolving organ dysfunction.

Isoflurane exposure can affect blood pressure, but mean dose in the immediate post-op window is an indirect and highly confounded marker for renal hypoperfusion. Early epoch effects are often transient and dominated by surgical/CPB factors.

Mean SvO2 reflects global oxygen delivery/consumption balance and can relate to renal hypoperfusion, but early post-op values are often transient and treatment-responsive. Mean is less sensitive than minima for detecting hypoperfusion insults.

High SvO2 peaks are generally not a trigger for AKI and may reflect high FiO2, sedation, or impaired extraction. Limited direct relevance to renal injury.

More frequent SvO2 checks can indicate concern for low cardiac output or shock, indirectly associated with AKI risk. Still a behavioral proxy, so kept <0.05.

Measurement frequency reflects clinician concern about oxygen delivery/low output, which can precede renal hypoperfusion, but it is not a physiologic value itself. Kept <0.05 per measured-feature rule.

Maintenance IV volume is a nonspecific proxy for fluid strategy and hemodynamic support; early post-op volumes are often protocolized and transient. Mean is also less informative than extremes for AKI risk.
Ongoing maintenance fluids may reflect evolving instability or attempts to optimize perfusion, indirectly related to AKI risk. Mean volume remains nonspecific and potentially collinear with max/min.

Closer to the outcome window, sustained maintenance fluid needs can indicate persistent vasoplegia/low effective circulating volume or attempts to treat oliguria. Still indirect and nonspecific, so kept low.

A high maximum maintenance IV rate early may reflect acute hypotension/vasoplegia management, which can contribute to renal hypoperfusion. Conservative scoring due to immediate post-bypass transience and epoch cap.

A higher peak maintenance IV rate in the trajectory phase may signal ongoing hemodynamic support needs and risk for renal hypoperfusion or fluid overload. Max is preferred over mean for capturing acute escalation, but remains indirect.

Late peak maintenance IV rate can indicate persistent instability or attempts to augment renal perfusion in response to oliguria, both associated with AKI risk. Max captures escalation better than mean/min, so slightly higher.
Minimum maintenance IV rate is weakly related to AKI and may reflect routine titration rather than pathology. Also likely collinear with mean/max and not a clear insult marker.
Low minimum maintenance IV rate is not a reliable indicator of renal hypoperfusion and may reflect routine weaning or fluid restriction. Weak and collinear with other volume summaries.

Frequency of documenting/ordering maintenance IV volume is largely routine in the immediate post-op period and not a physiologic driver. Kept very low per measured-feature rule.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects documentation intensity rather than renal physiology. Not a strong behavioral marker specific to impending AKI.
More frequent adjustments/recording late may reflect clinician concern about volume status or oliguria, indirectly linked to AKI risk. Still a behavioral proxy, so kept <0.05.

Having PAP systolic measured suggests invasive monitoring for cardiopulmonary instability, which can relate to renal hypoperfusion, but it is not the PAP value. Early post-op monitoring is common, so conservative.
Continued PAP monitoring into 13–24h may indicate persistent RV dysfunction/PH or shock risk, which can impair renal perfusion. Still a measurement-presence proxy, so kept low.

More frequent PAP monitoring late may indicate ongoing shock/right heart failure, which can contribute to renal congestion, but this is still an indirect behavioral signal. Kept low per rule for _measured features.
CVP measurement frequency reflects clinician concern for volume status/hemodynamics rather than a direct renal insult. Immediate post-bypass period is noisy, so predictive value is limited.
Increased CVP monitoring can indicate evolving RV failure/volume overload management, which is associated with renal venous congestion and AKI risk. Still a nonspecific proxy, so capped low.

Late increased CVP monitoring may signal persistent hemodynamic difficulty (congestion/vasopressor titration) that often precedes AKI in cardiac surgery patients. Remains a behavioral proxy, so kept <0.05.

Mean EtCO2 is influenced by ventilation settings and perfusion but is not a specific AKI predictor. Early post-op values are often driven by anesthesia/ventilator management rather than renal perfusion.

This reflects documentation/monitoring rather than tachyarrhythmia burden or shock. Any link to AKI is indirect via illness severity and is weak.
